Introduction

Sound visualization is widely used to study sound fields and to localize sound sources [1–2]. I covered the history of sound visualization at length in two earlier articles:

A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 1

A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 2

There are generally three measurement techniques for visualizing a sound field: step-by-step measurement, simultaneous measurement and scanning measurement. Considering measurement time, equipment cost and flexibility, scanning has the edge [3]. Scan & Paint moves a sound intensity probe (a microphone for sound pressure plus a Microflown sensor for particle velocity) through the sound field while a camera films the scan. Sound pressure, particle velocity or sound intensity are then obtained, directly or through an algorithm, and all three fields can be visualized [4–5]. The particle velocity and sound intensity fields are vector fields, which, compared with ordinary scalar fields, can simplify the analysis [6] and make it easy to pinpoint sources accurately even on site with high background noise. Here is the most direct way to get a feel for it:

For more on the particle velocity sensor, see this earlier article:

Particle velocity: there is more to sound than sound pressure

How scan-based imaging works

Scanning? What comes to mind is probably this, this and this:

Imaging? You’re probably thinking of that, that and that:

Reality is lean; acoustics is lavish. Buuut in acoustics, it actually looks like thiiis:

The probe is moved around the object under test to capture acoustic signals, and a camera tracks its path. The space the path runs through is then divided into cells, and each stretch of the path is assigned to its cell. In each cell, the acoustic signals recorded along that stretch of the path are processed, and the result represents the acoustic response of the cell. In a scalar field, it appears as a point with a certain strength; in a vector field, it is an arrow with both strength and a sense of direction. The key technologies of scan-based imaging are therefore probe tracking and spatial discretization.

3D scanning reconstructs the three-dimensional sound field. The principle is similar to 2D scanning; the differences lie in the probe and in how its path is tracked. The 3D system uses a 3D PU probe with three orthogonally mounted Microflown sensors and one microphone, so it captures 3D particle velocity; multiplied by the sound pressure, that gives 3D sound intensity. The camera is a 3D infrared camera: it emits infrared light, which reflective spheres attached to the probe bounce back to the camera, and from this the position and orientation of the probe in space are determined. The scan path can be generated in real time.

The 2D and 3D scanning systems

The two systems are called Scan & Paint 2D and Scan & Paint 3D, abbreviated here as S&P2D and S&P3D. They consist of the following equipment:

Their hardware gives them inherently different characteristics in four respects: the probe, the tracking, the scanning and the scan path. Both can measure sound pressure, particle velocity, sound intensity and sound power (given the area). The frequency range is 20–10,000 Hz. The figure-of-eight directivity of the Microflown sensor does not change, so the spatial resolution of neither system is affected; S&P3D can reach a resolution of 3 mm. S&P3D captures the probe path in real time, with no post-processing needed. Another notable difference: because S&P3D tracks the path in 3D, the probe can be moved freely during the scan without affecting the results, so it places very few demands on the operator.

Side by side in practice

A loudspeaker

Both systems accurately locate the three drivers, with similar results. The imaging plane lies 2 cm in front of the loudspeaker. For S&P3D the plane is chosen in post-processing, so as long as enough of the scan passes through that plane, repeatability is assured, which makes it suitable for comparative tests and benchmarking.

When a 3D view is needed, S&P2D cannot deliver a true one; instead, the camera has to be repositioned three times.

By combining near-field and far-field measurements, S&P3D can visualize the whole sound field and so reveal the loudspeaker’s directivity (if the measurement is made in an anechoic chamber).

Inside a car

Both systems can locate sound sources on a car dashboard. S&P3D is not constrained by the camera angle or the dimensions of the probe, so its results are more accurate and more intuitive.

Visualizing the sound field inside the car reveals the distribution of modes around the driver’s head. That gives car audio designers and automotive engineers a reference for improving the interior structure and the acoustic comfort. After all, the driver is king of the car! (Unless you are chauffeuring your boss.)

Conclusion

By scanning a sound field in 2D or 3D, scan-based imaging quickly and accurately reveals how the field is distributed and so locates the sources. It is widely used in automotive noise and vibration reduction, source localization and sound field design. S&P2D has the advantage of being inexpensive and fast, while S&P3D offers more accurate and comprehensive source localization.

I will present some of this at the National Acoustics Conference in Shenzhen, and I will also be at the automotive testing expo in Shanghai afterward. Looking forward to meeting those of you who will be there and want to say hello in person!
